messages.author: 97d82fedb7016adb
messages.subject: expose Stan model user functions to interfaces (rstan)
parts:
Hi!

Working more and more with the Stan functions, I find them just wonderful to do all my computation work in my models. Now it would be even better if we could call these functions somehow from R.

Currently, I have to write a model for inference and one for simulation. With the Stan functions these two models look very much the same and doing the simulation would easily be doable from R if I could somehow call the Stan user functions defined in the model.

It looks to me that almost everything is there, i.e. the Rcpp glue between Stan and R is fairly thin and this should be doable.

Could this be done in Stan/rstan generally?
As an intermediate solution: Can I make some declarations manually in order to access the Stan user functions via Rcpp? Has someone experience in that or even has done it?

Many thanks!

Best,
Sebastian

messages.author: 8aa9b8cc06fdc99c
messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] expose Stan model user functions to interfaces (rstan)
parts:
I think Jiqiang has a nifty solution that lets you
do just that. The last post is Feb 18 on a long thread
with subject: [stan-users] Re: Exposing functions via Rcpp

It's not in the current release, but should land
soon. There are some subtleties around the different kind of default
arguments (like functions ending in "_rng" needing to get a PRNG
passed in).

The big upside is that it would allow unit testing, which is
something we sorely need.

I don't think it's in the current release, but it should be going
in soon and I'm sure he'd share the code.

- Bob

messages.author: 97d82fedb7016adb
messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] expose Stan model user functions to interfaces (rstan)
parts:
Hi Ben!

WHOW!!! I tried it and it works like a charm... this is really a breakthrough for me.

Let me explain why: In my particular case I am dealing with PK (PD) problem which are notoriously complex models in the sense that it is very tedious to code them right. I assume the same arguments apply to any other more complex model. Now, the generated quantities block is a convenient place to do posterior checks, I agree. However, doing so glues together what does not necessarily has to go together which is inference and prediction. These are two different things and there are many reasons to do this in two steps:

- inference takes long, i.e. I worked with models which take 2-3 days per chain (noticing that I would need a different predictive check after two days hurts)
- to me there are two bits for prediction: first I want to predict my data I used to fit & (if I have) predict other external data to the model. Hence, this is anyway external to the model data set (and I often find more external data set when discussing with colleagues)
- then, after I have qualified my model, the fun part begins, which is "what-if", i.e. with PK problems I can start to ask - what if my next study is like XXX which forces me to simulate from the posterior
- even for fairly simple models this external prediction is very useful. Just imagine an unbalanced design for some covariates (let's say unbalanced due to problems here and there with sampling). By no means it is possible to foresee all those covariate combinations which may be of interest.

You are right that I need to watch out for random seeds, yes, but this I anyway have to do for any serious computation. In a nutshell, this makes the overall modelling process *much* more flexible as this allows me separate inference & prediction.

Some more comments:

- I would rename the function to something more general, to me this not just about testing a function, it is much more (flexible posterior simulation)
- You could go even further, i.e. you could create a function which takes as input everything from the data block and then provide the functions which correspond to the blocks, i.e.
* a transformed data block which would return a list of all transformed data variables (as a function of the input data)
* a transformed parameters function which takes as input the input data and all those parameters and returns the calculated transformed parameters
* a model function taking as input data & parameters (transformations can be automatically applied)

When is this functionality becoming part of the official rstan packages? Any time soon? I really hope so, just amazing!

Best,
Sebastian

messages.author: 743bbacc59f4b25f
messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] expose Stan model user functions to interfaces (rstan)
parts:
On Monday, March 2, 2015 at 6:16:27 PM UTC-5, Bob Carpenter wrote:

> On Monday, March 2, 2015 at 10:39:25 PM UTC+1, Ben Goodrich wrote:
>
> It would still entail two compilations because the C++ source used to expose the user-defined functions is a shortened and heavily modified version of the C++ source used to draw from the posterior.

Why does it need to be modified?  And how are you modifying it?

• It ignores everything starting with the class definition for the model (because that isn't relevant to the user-defined functions)
  • It takes away the local namespace (because Rcpp can only expose functions from the global namespace), which entails cutting all the using:: statements from what used to be the local namespace and pasting them inside the user-defined functions (so as not to create conflicts in the global namespace)
  • It gets rid of all the templating (because R can only use double or int)
  • All the user-defined functions that end in _rng have their arguments rewired to not pass a RNG& (because Rcpp can't deal with it). Instead they get an int& seed = 0 argument and at the first line of the body of the function is inserted as static boost::ecuyer1988 base_rng__(seed);. Thus, that gets initialized once with the initial seed but has global scope.
  • All the user-defined functions that end in _rng have their arguments rewired to not pass a T_lp_accum__& (because we can't template). Instead that is deleted and the first line of the body of the function is inserted as stan::math::accumulator<double> lp_accum__;.
  • All the user-defined functions have their arguments rewired to not pass a std::ostream* pstream__ (because Rcpp can't deal with it). Instead that is deleted and the first or second line of the body of the function is inserted as std::ostream* pstream__ = &Rcpp::Rcout;. Thus, if the user-defined function has print() statements, the Rcpp::Rcout thing makes sure they end up in R somehow.
  • All the inline declarations get taken away for some reason I can't remember (probably a Rcpp limitation)
  • The relevant functions (but not their declarations if there are declarations) get marked with the attribute // [[Rcpp::export]] before their definitions
  • A variety of things get deleted from the corresponding functors. Perhaps the functors themselves should be deleted because I don't think they can be called from R anyway.
  • Everything that looks like a templated type gets changed to a double, inclusive of all the internal const static bool propto__ = true; being changed to false so that (correct) log-density calculations will match those in R (if Stan is using the same parameterization)
  • There is some special handling of get_lp()
  • Dependencies are added to StanHeaders, BH, RcppEigen, and Rcpp so that it can find its #includes (because the compiler is not provided our ordinary CFLAGS)

That's all. So, yes it probably will be a nightmere to maintain, but all of that was a result of it first failing to compile without it. So, if that is the price that we have to pay for users to be able to test their user-defined functions (and Sebastian can do his posterior predictive stuff outside of generated quantities) then so be it. It would be good to have a test .stan file with every conceivable kind of valid user-defined function (Sebastian got 90% of the way there by himself), so that Travis or something could alert us when it inevitably gets broken. Ideally, as far as making something like this a feature that the other Stan interfaces could support, it would probably be better to have a flag that could be passed to stanc so that it would emit C++ code that would obviate the need for as many of the above tweaks as possible. But that would require a significant undertaking on the part of someone who understands stanc whereas my approach just requires a significant undertaking on the part of someone who understands regexes.

Ben

On Mon, Mar 2, 2015 at 5:54 PM, Ben Goodrich <goodri...@gmail.com> wrote:
On Monday, March 2, 2015 at 5:01:12 PM UTC-5, Sebastian Weber wrote:

It is easy to save them, but apparently impossible to use them after reloading in a different R session. If it were possible, it would fall on Rcpp to implement. If you have some NFS, my guess is the easiest way to speed up repeated compilations of the same thing would be to use the ccache wrapper to the C++ compiler.

Similar to use pakcage inline, ccache is not gonna work because some function name generated by Sourcecpp includes a randomly generated part.  For example, the following is the code generated from an example in sourceCpp. 

       #include <Rcpp.h>
       // [[Rcpp::export]]
       int fibonacci(const int x) {
         if (x == 0) return(0);
         if (x == 1) return(1);
         return (fibonacci(x - 1)) + fibonacci(x - 2);
       }

#include <Rcpp.h>
RcppExport SEXP sourceCpp_20489_fibonacci(SEXP xSEXP) {
BEGIN_RCPP
    SEXP __sexp_result;
    {
        Rcpp::RNGScope __rngScope;
        Rcpp::traits::input_parameter< const int >::type x(xSEXP );
        int __result = fibonacci(x);
        PROTECT(__sexp_result = Rcpp::wrap(__result));
    }
    UNPROTECT(1);
    return __sexp_result;
END_RCPP
}
